qs.q: A 60-year-old man who recently underwent antibiotic therapy for diverticulitis develops severe watery diarrhea and abdominal cramps. Stool assay detects a cytotoxin causing actin depolymerization. Which cellular target is modified by this toxin?
qs.e: Clostridium difficile toxin B glucosylates small Rho GTPases, causing actin cytoskeleton breakdown and pseudomembranous colitis.

ai.title: Acute Diverticulitis: Diagnosis and Management
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: Diverticulitis is inflammation of colonic outpockets (diverticula). It presents with abdominal pain, fever, and changes in bowel habit. Management ranges from conservative measures to surgery for complications like perforation.

sections.p: Diverticulitis is the inflammation or infection of small pouches (diverticula) that form in the lining of the digestive system, most commonly in the colon. These pouches are asymptomatic until they become inflamed or infected.
b: Diverticula are outpockets of colonic mucosa and submucosa through muscle layer weaknesses.
Diverticular disease is the presence of diverticula; diverticulitis is their inflammation.

sections.p: Severity is often classified using the Hinchey classification for complicated diverticulitis, which guides management, especially regarding surgical intervention.
b: Stage 0: Mildly inflamed diverticula, often treated conservatively.
Stage I: Pericolic inflammation or phlegmon.
Stage II: Pelvic abscess or intra-abdominal abscess.
Stage III: Purulent peritonitis.
Stage IV: Fecal peritonitis.

sections.p: The exact cause is unclear, but it's thought to involve increased intraluminal pressure, leading to microperforation and inflammation. Factors include low-fiber diet, obesity, and aging.
b: Low dietary fiber intake.
Increased colonic intraluminal pressure.
Fecal stasis.
Aging population.
Possible role of gut microbiota.

sections.p: The classic presentation is left iliac fossa pain, often with fever and a change in bowel habits. Patients may also experience nausea, vomiting, and localized tenderness.
b: Abdominal pain, typically LLQ.
Fever.
Nausea and vomiting.
Constipation or diarrhea.
Tenderness on palpation.

t.b: To assess for leukocytosis (raised white blood cells) as a sign of infection or inflammation.
To measure the level of inflammation in the body.
To look for signs of obstruction or free air (perforation).
Can sometimes visualize thickened bowel wall or abscesses, especially in resource-limited settings.
The gold standard for diagnosing diverticulitis, assessing severity, and identifying complications.

sections.p: Serious complications require urgent intervention and include perforation, abscess formation, bowel obstruction, and fistula formation.
b: Perforation: Leading to peritonitis and sepsis.
Abscess formation: Localized collection of pus.
Bowel obstruction: Due to inflammation or stricture.
Fistula formation: Abnormal connection between bowel and other organs (e.g., bladder, vagina).

sections.p: Treatment depends on severity. Uncomplicated cases are managed conservatively with antibiotics and bowel rest. Complicated cases may require percutaneous drainage or surgery.
b: Uncomplicated diverticulitis: Bowel rest (clear liquids), oral antibiotics (e.g., ciprofloxacin + metronidazole or amoxicillin-clavulanate).
Complicated diverticulitis (abscess): Percutaneous drainage and antibiotics.
Perforation/Peritonitis: Urgent surgical resection (e.g., sigmoid colectomy) with possible stoma.
Pain management with analgesics.
Intravenous fluids for hydration.

sections.p: After recovery, patients are advised on dietary changes and lifestyle modifications to prevent recurrence. Regular colonoscopy may be recommended.
b: High-fiber diet: Gradually increase fiber intake.
Adequate hydration.
Regular exercise.
Avoidance of NSAIDs.
Colonoscopy to rule out malignancy after resolution of acute episode.

sections.p: Several conditions can mimic diverticulitis, requiring careful differential diagnosis based on history, examination, and investigations.
b: Appendicitis: Typically RLQ pain, though can be atypical.
Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS): Chronic, relapsing symptoms without inflammation.
Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD - Crohn's, Ulcerative Colitis): Chronic inflammation with different patterns.
Colorectal cancer: Can present with similar symptoms, especially if obstructing.
Gynaecological conditions: Ovarian cysts, pelvic inflammatory disease.

sections.p: Certain findings can be misleading, making diagnosis challenging. It's crucial to correlate findings with the clinical picture.
b: Normal white blood cell count: Can occur in elderly or immunocompromised patients.
CT scan findings: Mild thickening can be seen in other conditions; clinical correlation is key.
Absence of diverticula on colonoscopy: May not have been performed during acute inflammation.

faq.q: Can diverticulitis be treated at home?
faq.a: Mild, uncomplicated diverticulitis can often be managed at home with rest, clear fluids, and oral antibiotics, but requires close medical supervision.

faq.q: What is the role of fiber in preventing diverticulitis?
faq.a: A high-fiber diet is thought to reduce the risk of diverticulitis by increasing stool bulk and reducing pressure in the colon.

faq.q: Is surgery always necessary for diverticulitis?
faq.a: No, surgery is typically reserved for complicated cases such as perforation, abscess, or recurrent severe episodes.

exam: A 65-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of left iliac fossa pain, fever, and constipation. On examination, he is pyrexial with localized tenderness in the LLQ. What is your immediate management plan? — Resuscitation (IV fluids, IV antibiotics), pain relief, NPO (nil by mouth), and investigations (FBC, CRP, consider CT scan).

What are the key differences in presentation and management between uncomplicated and complicated diverticulitis? — Uncomplicated: conservative (oral antibiotics, diet modification). Complicated: requires more aggressive treatment (IV antibiotics, drainage, surgery) for perforation, abscess, obstruction.

How would you differentiate diverticulitis from appendicitis in a patient presenting with abdominal pain? — Location of pain (LLQ vs RLQ), associated symptoms, and imaging findings (CT scan is definitive).

What are the potential complications of diverticulitis, and how does the Hinchey classification help in their management? — Complications include perforation, abscess, obstruction, fistula. Hinchey stages guide surgical vs. conservative/drainage management.

Why is a high-fiber diet recommended for patients with a history of diverticulitis? — To increase stool bulk, reduce colonic intraluminal pressure, and prevent stasis, thereby reducing the risk of new diverticula formation or inflammation.

You are managing a patient with a suspected diverticular abscess. What is the role of imaging and interventional radiology? — CT scan to confirm and localize the abscess. Interventional radiology for percutaneous drainage if the abscess is drainable and the patient is stable.

What are the indications for surgical resection in acute diverticulitis? — Perforation with generalized peritonitis, failure of conservative management, recurrent episodes, or complications like fistulae or strictures not amenable to other treatments.
